PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

...
## What your vote means
## Yes
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures.
For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
## No
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.

## Background
This measure requires the Insurance Commissioner (the Commissioner) to approve rates for certain types of health insurance.
The rate approval process would be similar to a process that is currently used for other types of insurance, such as automobile and homeowner's insurance.
Below, we provide background information on health insurance in California and automobile and homeowner's insurance rate regulation.
### Health Insurance in California
This measure mainly applies to individual and small group health insurance—which covers roughly 6 million Californians, or 16 percent of the population.
...

***Individual and Small Group Health Insurance Rates Must Be Approved by the Commissioner.*** The measure makes current and future individual and small group health insurance rates—including rates for health insurance that is regulated by CDI or DMHC—subject to the rate approval process established under Proposition 103.
The measure also states that rates proposed after November 6, 2012 must be approved by the Commissioner, and payments based on rates in effect on November 6, 2012 are subject to refund.

# Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
**DOWNWARD ARC —** Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.
Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots.
Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers.
Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians.
...
But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.

Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.”

45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.
